topics.topic: correcting the unit 2 tashkeel drills (8 and 10) word by word with students called on by name - where the fatHa, Damma, kasra and sukuun go on each dictated word, why the final short vowel is assumed rather than written, and her own syllable convention, which she flagged as differing from the book's: she pairs every consonant with its vowel, the book counts a consonant plus sukuun as one syllable, and she told the class to use whichever is easier. Also the reading technique she wants - read one syllable, go back to the start of the word, and chain forward again until you reach the end

drill 13 letter connection at the board - each student taking a word, writing the connected form on the right side while she corrected on the left, then reading it aloud. The recurring corrections were direction (one student was writing left to right), initial versus medial forms, and connection LENGTH: a connector drawn too long reads as a letter that has not been taught yet, so it has to stay dash-sized. She closed with the three handwriting styles she accepts for stacking a baa over a yaa, and her rule for all of them - she is not grading calligraphy, only whether she can read it, but she will correct a yaa that is not curvy and a baa that is not long, because in running text the dots alone are not enough to tell letters apart

drill 17, two recorded dialogues worked phrase by phrase, one Egyptian and one Levantine, played whole first and then stopped every few words - ahlan preferred over marHaba as the Egyptian opener, the biki/fiki split with the point that the FEMININE form does not change between dialects while the masculine takes a sukuun rather than a fatHa on the kaaf, HaDretak versus HaDretik as the polite 'your name' and how it maps onto the HaDratuka/HaDratuki they already learned, and the local shorthand where Masr means Cairo and ash-Sham means Damascus, plus Iskandariyya and Halab. Two culture questions from the class came off the video as well

the letter jiim, taught alone and deliberately - the triangle that drops below the line with one dot beneath, the two printed fonts (the triangle against the gapped form), all four positional shapes including the zigzag medial form, whether the connection sits on or above the line, and three practice words built letter by letter on the board. She held Haa and Khaa back to Thursday on purpose because all three look alike

announcements.text: DRILL 15 IS AN ORAL ASSESSMENT AND IT IS DUE NEXT TUESDAY (2026-09-15). 'Drill 15 will be your oral assessment and it is due next Tuesday... And it is due on Tuesday, next Tuesday.' It is basic greetings built only from vocabulary already taught - she asks marHaba, you answer; she asks how you are, you answer. She will explain the format in class on Thursday but told the class they can start listening now. She named NO clock time and NO platform.

HOMEWORK 1 AND 2 WERE WORTH 20 POINTS EACH AND SOME STUDENTS SCORED 1. She spent several minutes on it and told everyone to go back and look: 'You're supposed to receive 20 for homework one and homework 2... So if you receive one, look at my notes.' Every failure she listed was completeness, not correctness - not finding drill 13 at all, doing 5 of the 11 words because they did not turn the page, and submitting the book half without the Lingco half.

WHAT 'GRADED FOR COMPLETION' ACTUALLY MEANS, stated plainly for the first time: she checks BOTH platforms and both must be complete. 'when we look into the instruction, I have to see all the drills on Lingo and on Canvas submitted.' Lingco showing 100 percent plus the right number of drills photographed onto Canvas equals full marks automatically. You do NOT need to screenshot the Lingco work onto Canvas - she called that extra work you do not have to do.

Homework 3 is unit 3: four drills photographed to Canvas plus one on Lingco. She listed it twice a minute apart and the two lists do not match word for word - first 'drill one, two and five on canvas' with drill 3 on Lingco and drill 4 (letter connection, like drill 13) in the book, then 'this homework will include one, two, three, and four on Canvas and one on Lingo'. The reading that satisfies both is Canvas drills 1, 2, 4 and 5 with drill 3 on Lingco. NO DUE DATE WAS SPOKEN, so nothing is emitted to the due list.

Label every submission with the drill number, homework number and unit number - a standing rule now in its third class. New today: she thanked the students who used highlighters to mark which drill is which, and said it made grading noticeably faster. Failing that, just make it readable.

Tashkeel is not graded, restated for the third class running and this time with the boundary drawn precisely: she does not deduct for it on homework OR exams, she will still correct an obvious mistake, and she will not stop anyone who wants to write it because they need it to read correctly. The goal is reading without it, the way street signs, newspapers and shop signs are written. She also noted that photographs of homework often lose the marks anyway.

A FREE NATIVE-SPEAKER TUTOR IS NOW AVAILABLE. Fabiola, enrolled in 101 but already advanced and Egyptian, will tutor, check homework before submission, and practise speaking. Her email is written on the board and she may group two or three students into one appointment. Khouri pressed twice that she will not do the work for you and that students should not all descend on her the week of the exam: 'don't wait until everybody, like before the exam and then you call her. Give her a chance.'

Drill 16 (the major cities of Syria and Egypt) is self-study and is not submitted - background so the place names in the book's videos make sense. 'those on your own, do those on your own to just learn extra about the region.'

Thursday's plan, stated at the end: she teaches Haa and Khaa (which look like jiim), covers the reading on shaking hands and physical greeting, and explains the drill 15 oral assessment. She taught jiim alone today on purpose - 'I need to introduce you to a letter, jiim, today in order just to give you some time to process.'

There is no separate letter for the 'a' sound yet - both the e and a sounds heard in the listening exercises are written with kasra, and which one a word takes is learned case by case rather than by rule. She said she will start correcting the distinction later and that for now pronouncing everything as e is fine. She ran listening exercise 11 (page 38) unplanned to demonstrate it.

position.next: Haa and Khaa on Thursday, the shaking-hands reading, and drill 15 as the oral assessment due Tuesday
position.said: 'this is unit 3, okay? So today we're going to start with unit 3. We'll finish, well, we have to finish from unit 2 and we'll start with unit 3'... Most of the hour was still unit 2 cleanup - drills 8, 10, 13, listening exercise 11 on page 38, and drill 17. Unit 3 was entered at the end, through the new letter and through homework 3.

commitments.title: Before Thursday: practise writing jiim in all four positions and start unit 3 drill 1, and read the Alif Baa paragraph on shaking hands - Thursday she teaches Haa and Khaa, which look like jiim, and covers the greeting etiquette
Unit 2 drill 15 oral assessment - spoken basic greetings using only the vocabulary taught so far; she explains the format in class on Thursday

off_slide: Introduced Fabiola to the class in person and asked her to give her background; she is Egyptian and already fluent but shy about being put on the spot, so Khouri did most of the talking and had her write her email on the board

Answered Parker directly three times: on hearing the difference between a fatHa and a sukuun (she demonstrated 'ta / t' against 'ta ta' until he could hear it), on whether tashkeel must now be written on everything from here on, and on why the speakers in the video repeat the welcome three times

Ran listening exercise 11 on page 38 unplanned, purely because a student said the a and e sounds were hard to separate at speed - and walked all six items, marking which are closer to a and which to e even though both are written with kasra

The two culture answers she gave off the drill 17 video: how close a man may sit to a woman depends entirely on which part of the Arab world you are in, you never approach a hijabi woman that way, and you never ask someone of the opposite sex for a phone number directly - it goes through a friend, or you overhear it, or you find a pretext to need it
Why the video repeats the welcome: repetition IS the emphasis, and hospitality requires it - 'if one of you is visiting me in my home, I have to be very welcoming'

That native speakers swallow vowels and run syllables together at speed in every language, including English - and her own experience learning English, which is why she asks students to speak slowly and loudly to her

That she is teaching a system that does not exist in Arabic on purpose: 'we don't have this system, American system or Latin languages... So we are creating our own system to help you think similarly like English'

Her longer-term goal for the class, stated as a stage they will reach rather than a rule: reading from context without tashkeel, deciding from who you are speaking to whether a word is anta or anti. She said she has already started pushing the 201 students that way
That HaDritak literally means 'your presence', and that in Egypt it is also used sarcastically
The word she finished the hour on was 'beige' - the colour, borrowed straight into Arabic - written out to practise jiim

I want to get you into a stage where you could read like an Arab, without tashki[l]. You would look at the word from the context, you would know this word is [which]. That's my goal. But it's going to take us a few stages.

notes: THE HEADLINE IS A GRADED ITEM THAT EXISTS NOWHERE ELSE: drill 15 is an ORAL assessment due next Tuesday, 2026-09-15. She said 'next Tuesday' twice, so the date is solid. She named neither a clock time nor a platform, so the commitment carries 23:59 and where 'other'. She explains the format in class on Thursday, which is the moment to pin down where it gets submitted - an oral task almost certainly lives on the audio-capable platform (Lingco) rather than as a Canvas photo, but she did not say that and this record does not claim it.

SECOND ACTION: go look at the homework 1 and 2 grades. She said outright that some students received 1 point where 20 was available, and that the cause is always a missing piece rather than a wrong answer - most often the Lingco half, or the second page of drill 13. Her Canvas comments say which. Full marks are automatic once both platforms are complete, so a 1 is recoverable information rather than a lost cause.

HOMEWORK 3 HAS NO SPOKEN DUE DATE. The 9/3 record has the weekly homework due on a Friday, which would make this Friday 2026-09-11, but she did not say it today, so nothing is emitted. Worth confirming from Canvas or Lingco rather than assuming the pattern held.

Homework 3's composition is recorded as the reconciliation of two lists she gave a minute apart, not as a verbatim instruction: Canvas drills 1, 2, 4 and 5, plus drill 3 on Lingco. The count in her second pass ('four on Canvas and one on Lingo') matches that reading, but check the Canvas assignment text before trusting the drill numbers.

The course is now slightly AHEAD of the ledger plan. The plan puts unit 3 in week 4 beginning 2026-09-14; she opened unit 3 today, 9/8, with jiim and with homework 3. Most of the hour was still unit 2 cleanup, so the position token is unit 3 on the strength of the new letter and the new homework rather than on how the time was spent.

Two conventions now differ between her and the book, and she said to follow whichever is easier: she pairs each consonant with its vowel as one syllable, the book (in unit 3) ends a syllable at the sukuun. Expect the book's syllable counts in unit 3 not to match hers.

A free native-speaker tutor now exists and she asked people to use her EARLY rather than the week before the exam. Given how this course is graded - completion, checked across two platforms, corrected out loud in class - the highest-value use is having homework checked before submitting, which is exactly the failure mode that cost people 19 points on homework 1 and 2.

FOR CARD-MAKING, NOT FOR THIS RECORD: a large block of today's content is Egyptian-dialect pronunciation (ahlan biki, HaDratik, Masr for Cairo). The standing rule is that Egyptian audio does not go onto Anki cards. The Levantine half of drill 17 is Khouri's own dialect and is fair game; the Egyptian half is lecture context only.

Transcript garbles read through rather than quoted - this file is by far the worst of the four for Arabic terms, and nothing in it should be quoted verbatim as her wording: 'Teshki' / 'Tashki' / 'Tishki' / 'the skill' / 'seclude' all for tashkeel, 'the four machine' for the four Harakaat, 'but how' for fatHa, 'the old ski' / 'supoon' / 'succoon' for sukuun, 'Castra' / 'kestra' / 'kisser' for kasra, 'domo' / 'dama' / 'demma' for Damma, 'the drill aids' for drill 8, 'Jude 13' for drill 13, 'Hariff Jean' / 'theem' / 'Zhim' / 'the sheet' / 'gene' all for jiim, 'the how and the tha' for Haa and Khaa, 'LF' and 'Alice' for alif, 'bad' / 'bar' / 'batasa' for baa, 'Bika' / 'beak' / 'big' / 'Becky' for biki and bika, 'Hadratic' / 'Hadertek' / 'Hadratouki' for HaDratik, HaDretek and HaDratuki, 'Skanderia' for Iskandariyya, 'Minina' / 'Menway' / 'Minwen' for min wayn, 'Annamen Halab' for ana min Halab, 'Rose Junk' and 'Stone' unrecoverable. Student names are mangled too - both 'Barker' and 'Parker' appear for Parker.

The Thursday commitment is marked inferred rather than explicit because the transcript is garbled at the exact sentence ('Practice theem on Thursday, because I'm going to teach you also the how and the tha'). The reading taken here - practise jiim BEFORE Thursday, because Haa and Khaa arrive Thursday and look identical - is the only one the 'because' clause supports. The shaking-hands reading in the same commitment is clean and explicit: 'now read the paragraph about shaking hands. I'll talk about it next time.' She named no page or unit for it.
